02 — Overview

How tool calling works, in general. Read this before you write code.

The protocol has three moves

A model cannot read a file. It can only produce text. Tool calling works because both sides agree that certain text is a request:

  1. Advertise. The request carries a list of tool schemas: a name, a

description, and the shape of the arguments.

  1. Call. The model's reply contains a structured call instead of prose: an

id, a name, and an arguments string.

  1. Return. The client runs the tool and appends a message that names the id

it answers. Then it asks the model again.

The pairing is the contract. A tool result carries the id of the call it answers, and providers reject a conversation where a call has no result or a result has no call. Everything else in this chapter follows from that rule.

Why the arguments arrive in pieces

The reply streams, so the call streams with it. The first fragment for a call carries its index, id and name. Later fragments carry only the index and a piece of the arguments string:

data: {"choices":[{"delta":{"tool_calls":[{"index":0,"id":"call_1","type":"function","function":{"name":"read","arguments":""}}]}}]}
data: {"choices":[{"delta":{"tool_calls":[{"index":0,"function":{"arguments":"{\"pa"}}]}}]}
data: {"choices":[{"delta":{"tool_calls":[{"index":0,"function":{"arguments":"th\":\"a."}}]}}]}
data: {"choices":[{"delta":{"tool_calls":[{"index":0,"function":{"arguments":"txt\"}"}}]}}]}
  fragment 1:  index 0 · id call_1 · name read      ← identity
  fragment 2:  index 0 · arguments `{"pa`           ← no id, no name
  fragment 3:  index 0 · arguments `th":"a.`
  fragment 4:  index 0 · arguments `txt"}`
                                                    ────────────────
  result:      one call, arguments `{"path":"a.txt"}`

Folding by index is the only reliable rule. Folding by id works until the second fragment arrives with an empty id, which is every real provider.

A model may also return several calls in one message. Each has its own index, and the results must be returned in the same order.

Failure is a result, not an exception

The model's arguments are text it wrote, so they can be wrong. A path can be missing, a file can be huge, a path can climb out of the workspace, and the JSON itself can be malformed.

None of those should end the program. Each becomes a tool result with an error flag, so the model can read the message and try something else:

SituationResult the model seesProgram
file missingno such file: nope.txtcontinues, exit 0
arguments malformedarguments are not valid JSON: {"path":continues, exit 0
path escapes the workspacepath escapes the workspace: ../../etc/passwdcontinues, exit 0
file larger than the limitfirst 20,000 bytes + a truncation markercontinues, exit 0

The exception is a broken request to the provider, which is not the model's fault and cannot be repaired by asking again.

Two things the model cannot do

It cannot see the workspace. Everything it knows about a file comes from a tool result. That is why a truncation marker matters: without it, the model believes it read the whole file and will answer confidently about the part it never saw.

It cannot recover from a silent failure. A tool that returns an empty string on error teaches the model that the file is empty. Say what happened.

Where this chapter stops

This program makes one hop: call, run tools, ask once more, print. If the model asks for a second tool after the first result, the program prints whatever text came with that request and stops.

That limit is deliberate. Chapter 04 replaces the hop with a loop, and the difference between the two is easier to see when you have written the hop.
